blocks.text: Quick verdict

Rayobyte is the better value for scraping at any real volume: 10 GB costs $35 against IPRoyal's $52.50, and its price drops to $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte, with traffic that never expires. IPRoyal is the better choice when you need SOCKS5 (Rayobyte's residential network is HTTP(S) only), sticky sessions of up to seven days for account work, or a 1 GB starting purchase. Teams that also want datacenter proxies will find Rayobyte's catalog stronger.

IPRoyal and Rayobyte are among the few providers whose residential traffic never expires, which makes them natural rivals for irregular workloads. Beyond that shared policy, they differ a lot. Rayobyte's volume bands get much cheaper as you scale, down to $0.90/GB, but its residential gateway does not support SOCKS5. IPRoyal costs more at volume but supports SOCKS5 and sticky sessions up to seven days. This comparison shows where each one's pricing and features win.

blocks.text: IPRoyal in 2026: what you get

IPRoyal built its reputation on flexible, non-expiring residential bandwidth and straightforward pricing. The pool is smaller than the enterprise networks at 32M+ advertised IPs, but it covers 195 countries, supports SOCKS5, and offers some of the longest sticky sessions available (up to seven days). Its headline $1.75/GB rate only applies at 10 TB; most buyers will pay between $5 and $7 per GB on small orders.

Strengths: Residential traffic that does not expire; Sticky sessions up to 7 days; Can start with a single gigabyte; Several proxy types plus Web Unblocker in one account. Weak spots: Smaller pool than the enterprise networks; Headline $1.75/GB rate needs a 10 TB purchase; Mid-volume prices are not published.
Rayobyte in 2026: what you get

Rayobyte combines one of the strongest datacenter proxy catalogs with a simple residential offer. Residential traffic is bought in volume bands, from $3.50/GB below 50 GB down to $0.90/GB at a terabyte, and it never expires. Users often praise its human support team. The trade-offs are HTTP-only residential access and limited public data on pool size.

Strengths: Non-expiring residential traffic; Steep volume discounts down to $0.90/GB; Excellent datacenter and ISP catalog; Well-regarded human support. Weak spots: No SOCKS5 or UDP on residential; Pool size not prominently published; Fewer advanced targeting options than enterprise providers.
Pricing: IPRoyal vs Rayobyte

IPRoyal's residential subscription costs $7 for 1 GB, $11.90 for 2 GB and $52.50 for 10 GB ($5.25/GB); pay-as-you-go is 5% more ($7.35 for 1 GB). The advertised $1.75/GB rate applies only at 10 TB. Prices for custom volumes such as 25, 100 or 500 GB are calculated in the dashboard.
Rayobyte prices residential traffic in four pay-as-you-go bands: $3.50/GB for 1-49 GB, $2/GB for 50-249 GB, $1.50/GB for 250-999 GB and $0.90/GB for 1-5 TB. Traffic does not expire.

At 10 GB a month, Rayobyte is the cheaper option at about $35 against $52.50 for IPRoyal, roughly 33% less. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because IPRoyal does not publish an exact price for that volume; Rayobyte comes to about $200. Neither provider makes you use it or lose it: both IPRoyal and Rayobyte let unused traffic carry forward, so the comparison really comes down to rate and features.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

Rayobyte does not publish a clear residential pool figure, so a size comparison is not possible on published data. IPRoyal lists '32M+' and Rayobyte lists 'Not prominently published'. In practice, what matters is how many unique IPs you get in the countries you target, which you can measure in a short trial by sending a few thousand requests and counting distinct exit addresses. For coverage, IPRoyal lists 195 countries and Rayobyte lists Global. On targeting, IPRoyal offers country, state and city (ISP selection needs verification), while Rayobyte offers country, region and city.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Protocol support is a real difference here. IPRoyal supports HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS5, while Rayobyte offers HTTP, HTTPS (no SOCKS5 on residential). If your tooling needs SOCKS5, for example some anti-detect browsers, desktop apps or non-HTTP traffic, that settles it in IPRoyal's favour. On sessions, IPRoyal offers rotating or sticky sessions from 1 second up to 7 days, and Rayobyte offers rotates per request by default; sticky sessions available. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With IPRoyal: solid success rates and non-expiring traffic for bursty crawls. With Rayobyte: cheap volume bands and traffic that never expires. Run the same small test on both before committing.

SERP and rank tracking: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. IPRoyal: it works, but it has no dedicated SERP product. Rayobyte: usable, with no dedicated SERP product. Let price and the countries you need decide.

Social media and multi-account management: IPRoyal wins. The deciding factor for IPRoyal: 7-day sticky sessions keep one IP on one account. The limitation on the Rayobyte side: no SOCKS5 limits some account tools.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With IPRoyal: city targeting with pay-only-for-what-you-use traffic. With Rayobyte: city targeting and low prices at volume. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Ad verification and geo-testing: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With IPRoyal: decent coverage but no ASN or carrier targeting on standard accounts. With Rayobyte: fewer carrier or ASN controls. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Tight budgets: close call. Both are reasonable choices here. IPRoyal: small entry purchases and traffic that never expires. Rayobyte: $2/GB from 50 GB and $0.90/GB at a terabyte. Let price and the countries you need decide.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. IPRoyal: No general free trial; Enterprise trial for verified companies. Rayobyte: Check current offer. Verification and payment rules differ too. IPRoyal: Optional ID verification; required for ISP-level targeting and PayPal. Rayobyte: Standard verification; US company. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test IPRoyal and Rayobyte before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle IPRoyal vs Rayobyte faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (IPRoyal: no general free trial; Enterprise trial for verified companies; Rayobyte: check current offer).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, IPRoyal comes out ahead in 1, Rayobyte in 0, and 5 are ties. That makes IPRoyal the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: IPRoyal is strongest for irregular or seasonal projects, while Rayobyte is strongest for mid-to-high volume scraping on a budget. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
